summary.text: A space station is a spacecraft that remains in orbit and hosts humans for extended periods, making it an artificial satellite with habitation facilities.
Most often stations have been research stations, but they have also served military or commercial uses, such as hosting space tourists.
The first was Salyut 1 in 1971, and today the International Space Station and China's Tiangong Space Station are the two fully operational ones.

facts.label: First station
facts.value: Salyut 1, launched by the Soviet Union in 1971

facts.label: Operating now
facts.value: The ISS and China's Tiangong Space Station

facts.label: Crowd record
facts.value: 17 people on all stations at once, May 30, 2023

facts.label: Design
facts.value: Often modular, built through docking ports

facts.label: Early designs
facts.value: Launched in one piece with all supplies aboard

items.prompt: A station is assembled from separate pieces. What do its docking ports let it do?

options.label: Leave its orbit and travel on between the planets
Join modules and take in visiting craft that swap people and supplies
Stay steady in space without needing any thrusters
Spin the whole station to create artificial gravity

items.explain: Docking ports allow modules to join and other spacecraft to dock for the exchange of people, supplies and tools.

items.prompt: A space station generally stays in its orbit. What are its thrusters for?

options.label: Keeping the station where it should be, called station keeping
Flying it away to other bodies
Chasing visiting spacecraft to bring them in
Turning it to face the Sun

items.explain: Stations generally do not leave their orbit, but they have thrusters for station keeping.

items.prompt: A crew in an early one-piece station used up the last of its supplies. What then happened to the station?

options.label: Cargo craft kept resupplying it
A second crew moved in and rebuilt it
It was extended with a new module
The station was abandoned

items.explain: Early stations were launched whole with their supplies, and after the supplies had been consumed the station was abandoned.

items.prompt: Salyut 6 and 7 had two docking ports instead of one. What did the extra port make possible?

options.label: Space tourists paying to visit the station for fun
Moving the whole station into a new and higher orbit
Visiting crews and supply craft, so people could stay on board
Launching the whole station again in a single piece

items.explain: The second port let a second crew visit and let Progress supply vehicles dock, so a crew could man the station continually.

items.prompt: Which order did these skills first appear on the road to building stations?

options.label: Rendezvous, then docking, then moving astronauts between docked ships
Docking, then rendezvous, then moving astronauts between ships
Moving astronauts between ships, then docking, then rendezvous
Rendezvous, then moving astronauts between ships, then docking

items.explain: Gemini first rendezvoused in 1965, Gemini 8 docked in 1966, and Apollo 9 made the first internal transfer in 1969.

items.prompt: Shortly before it was abandoned, Salyut 7 'hard docked' with a TKS tug. What did that test point toward?

options.label: Re-boosting a station into a higher orbit
Building stations from modules
Returning crews to Earth faster
Sending stations to the Moon

items.explain: It served as a proof of concept for the use of modular space stations.
